choices.text: Summer water was 19 C, 8 degrees warmer than spring water.
Fall was the warmest season.
Winter was the warmest season.
Spring water was warmer than summer water.

questions.explanation: Summer's 19 C is the highest reading, and 19 minus 11 is 8. The other choices reverse the ranking.

distractor_rationales.B: Fall measured 14 C, below summer's 19 C.
distractor_rationales.C: Winter measured 6 C, the coldest reading.
distractor_rationales.D: Spring measured 11 C, below summer's 19 C.

questions.stimulus: In a coastal estuary, conservation crews installed low fences of woven branches along the edge of a tidal marsh. The fences slow incoming water just enough for suspended sediment to settle. Within three seasons the marsh surface had risen several centimeters, keeping pace with the local rise in sea level. Crews now treat the fences as temporary scaffolding: once grasses anchor the new sediment, the structures rot away.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A modest intervention can help a marsh build elevation fast enough to keep up with rising water.
Woven fences are the only way to restore a coastal marsh.
Grasses grow faster than sea level rises in every estuary.
Suspended sediment is unimportant to the health of a marsh.

questions.explanation: The passage describes a low-cost fence that traps sediment, raises the marsh surface, and lets grasses take over. That makes a modest intervention the central point.

distractor_rationales.B: The text presents one technique, not a claim of exclusivity.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage describes one estuary keeping pace, not every estuary.
distractor_rationales.D: The entire mechanism depends on trapped sediment.

questions.stimulus: When a county archive began recording oral histories of retired dockworkers, staff wrote the summaries themselves. The transcripts were accurate but flat, stripped of the jokes and nicknames that carried meaning for the speakers. The archive then invited community members to annotate the recordings. Those notes identified people, places, and turns of phrase that outsiders had missed, and later researchers relied on them heavily.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Inviting community members to annotate recordings improved the archive's records in ways staff alone could not.
The archive's original transcripts contained factual errors.
Oral histories should replace written documents in county archives.
Later researchers ignored the archive's annotations.

questions.explanation: The passage says the staff transcripts were accurate but missed local meaning, and that community notes supplied what outsiders had missed. That is the central claim.

distractor_rationales.B: The text calls the transcripts accurate, not wrong.
distractor_rationales.C: No comparison with written documents is made.
distractor_rationales.D: The text says researchers relied on the notes heavily.

questions.stimulus: Paper mills in one region experimented with fibers from an invasive reed that clogs waterways. The reed broke down into pulp with less energy than wood, and the resulting paper was sturdy enough for packaging. Mills still cannot use the reed for fine writing paper because its fibers are short. Even so, harvesting the reed for packaging both lowered the cost of clearing waterways and produced a saleable product.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Using an invasive reed for packaging can yield a useful product while helping control the plant.
Invasive reeds are suitable for every kind of paper product.
Mills have stopped clearing waterways because of the reed.
Short fibers make a paper stronger than long fibers do.

questions.explanation: The passage sets out one limitation, fine paper, and then states the double benefit of using the reed for packaging. The main idea is that practical use and control can go together.

distractor_rationales.B: The text explicitly says the reed cannot be used for fine writing paper.
distractor_rationales.C: Harvesting the reed lowered clearing costs rather than stopping the work.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage treats short fibers as the reason fine paper is impossible.

questions.stimulus: Biologists tracking foxes in a large city found that animals living near busy roads shifted most of their activity to the hours after midnight. In quieter neighborhoods, the same species remained active at dusk. The shift did not follow temperature or food availability, both of which were similar across the sites studied.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Foxes living near heavy traffic appear to adjust when they are active.
Foxes avoid cities entirely when roads are busy.
Temperature determines when foxes leave their dens.
Food availability explains the difference between the sites.

questions.explanation: The passage reports a timing difference that tracks road traffic and rules out temperature and food. The central point is that the animals shift their active hours.

distractor_rationales.B: The foxes were living in the city, not avoiding it.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says temperature was similar across sites and did not explain the shift.
distractor_rationales.D: Food availability was also similar and is explicitly ruled out.

questions.stimulus: A poet working in a signed language composes by filming sequences rather than writing lines. Rhymes in this poetry are formed by repeating handshapes or locations in space, and a single sign can be held to mark a pause. Readers of a printed gloss often miss these patterns because the notation records words, not movement.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The visual structure of signed poetry is lost when the work is transcribed as words.
Signed poetry does not use rhyme of any kind.
Printed glosses make signed poems easier to understand.
Poets who sign avoid filming their work.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that rhyme lives in handshapes and held signs, which word-based notation does not capture. That is the central observation about transcription.

distractor_rationales.B: The text describes rhyme formed by repeated handshapes and locations.
distractor_rationales.C: It says readers of printed glosses often miss the patterns.
distractor_rationales.D: The poet composes by filming sequences.

questions.stimulus: Chemists analyzed trace elements in glass beads from several ancient ports. Beads from one harbor shared a chemical signature with sand from a river hundreds of kilometers inland, while beads from a neighboring harbor matched a coastal source. The pattern suggests that finished beads moved along routes separate from those that carried raw materials.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Chemical signatures in the beads suggest that trade in finished goods followed different routes from trade in raw materials.
All of the beads were made from a single source of sand.
Glassmaking began at the coast and spread inland.
The harbors were abandoned once the beads arrived.

questions.explanation: The beads match sources that do not match their own harbors, and the passage draws exactly that conclusion about separate routes. The other choices go beyond or contradict the evidence.

distractor_rationales.B: Two distinct source signatures are described.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says nothing about where glassmaking began.
distractor_rationales.D: No claim is made about the harbors being abandoned.

questions.stimulus: A seed bank is often imagined as a freezer full of envelopes. In practice, staff test germination every few years, because viability falls at different rates for different species. A batch that still sprouts at 80 percent may be left alone; one that falls below a threshold is regrown in a nursery so fresh seed can be stored.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Maintaining a seed bank requires ongoing testing and renewal, not just storage.
Freezers destroy the seeds they are meant to protect.
All species lose viability at the same rate.
Seed banks store only seeds of food crops.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the freezer image with the regular testing and nursery regrowth that keep a collection alive. That contrast is the main idea.

distractor_rationales.B: Freezing is not described as harmful, only as insufficient on its own.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says viability falls at different rates for different species.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage never limits seed banks to food crops.

questions.stimulus: Keepers of coastal lighthouses recorded weather every few hours for decades, noting wind, fog, and ice in bound volumes. Historians once treated these logs as background color. Climate scientists now digitize them, because the entries predate most instrumental records and describe conditions at headlands that no weather station covered.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Routine records kept for one purpose can become valuable evidence for another.
Lighthouse keepers were trained as climate scientists.
Continuous instrumental records are older than the logs.
The logs are valuable mainly for their descriptions of shipwrecks.

questions.explanation: The logs were routine weather notes for lighthouse work and are now a climate data source. That change in use is the passage's central point.

distractor_rationales.B: No such training is mentioned; the logs were simply kept routinely.
distractor_rationales.C: The text says the logs predate most instrumental records.
distractor_rationales.D: Shipwrecks are not mentioned at all.

questions.stimulus: In a rehearsal, a quartet stopped midway through a piece. Instead of naming a chord, the pianist hummed a phrase and tapped the ride cymbal. The bassist nodded, and the group restarted with a different feel. Later, the musicians said they rarely discuss harmony in words; the sound itself carries the instruction.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The musicians often communicate musical changes through sound rather than verbal explanation.
The quartet avoids rehearsing altogether.
The pianist is the group's formal director.
The bassist misunderstood the pianist's cue.

questions.explanation: The pianist conveys a change by humming and tapping, and the musicians say words are rarely needed. That is the central idea about how they communicate.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage shows a rehearsal in progress.
distractor_rationales.C: Nothing in the text establishes a formal director.
distractor_rationales.D: The bassist nods and the group restarts successfully.

questions.stimulus: Drilling an ice core yields a cylinder of layered snow. Each summer layer carries dust blown from continents, and the amount varies with wind strength and storm frequency. By counting layers and measuring dust, researchers reconstruct centuries of atmospheric circulation, even though no one recorded the weather at the time.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Dust in ice-core layers provides a record of past atmospheric circulation.
Ice cores record only the temperature of past summers.
All dust in an ice core comes from the ocean.
The layers cannot be counted reliably.

questions.explanation: The passage explains how counted layers and measured dust reveal past winds even without written records. That reconstruction is the main idea.

distractor_rationales.B: The text focuses on dust and circulation, not only summer temperature.
distractor_rationales.C: It says the dust was blown from continents.
distractor_rationales.D: Layer counting is the method the researchers rely on.

questions.stimulus: A weaving cooperative began attaching a small tag to each blanket naming the weaver and the pattern's origin. Buyers had previously chosen by color alone. After the tags appeared, orders shifted toward patterns whose stories customers could read, and younger weavers began learning designs that had nearly gone unused.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Sharing the story behind a pattern changed which designs buyers chose and renewed interest in them.
Buyers preferred blankets with no visible pattern.
The tags caused prices to fall sharply.
Older weavers stopped teaching their designs.

questions.explanation: The passage links the tags to a shift in orders and to younger weavers learning neglected designs. That is the central point about visible provenance.

distractor_rationales.B: Orders shifted toward patterned work with stories attached.
distractor_rationales.C: Prices are never mentioned.
distractor_rationales.D: Younger weavers began learning designs that had gone unused.

questions.stimulus: A historian compared two sixteenth-century maps of the same coastline. One shows a wide estuary; the other omits it and places a headland in its stead. The historian argues that the second map was copied from the first but corrected using a sailor's sketch, which recorded the headland after a storm had closed the estuary mouth.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The maps' disagreement may reflect a real change in the coastline rather than a copying error.
Both maps were drawn from the same survey.
The estuary never existed and was invented by a mapmaker.
The second map is simply a careless copy of the first.

questions.explanation: The historian's argument is that the coastline itself changed between surveys, so both maps can be right. That is the passage's central claim.

distractor_rationales.B: The text says the second map was corrected from a different sketch.
distractor_rationales.C: The estuary appears on the earlier map and is described as having been closed by a storm.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage argues against treating the difference as an error.

questions.stimulus: Hives kept on city rooftops often produce as much honey as hives in surrounding farmland. The reason seems to be variety: parks, balconies, and vacant lots supply flowers in succession from spring to fall, while a single field may bloom for only a few weeks. Beekeepers who plant for continuous bloom report steadier yields.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A range of flowers available over a long season can support urban hives.
Urban honey always tastes better than farm honey.
Farmland has no bees at all.
Rooftop hives need less care than rural hives.

questions.explanation: The passage attributes urban yields to flowers blooming in succession across many small spaces. That variety is the main explanation offered.

distractor_rationales.B: Taste is not discussed.
distractor_rationales.C: Farmland is described as having fields that bloom briefly, not as lacking bees.
distractor_rationales.D: The amount of care is never compared.

questions.stimulus: When a small theater replaced its incandescent fixtures with LEDs, rehearsals changed. Actors could suddenly see the audience, and directors began blocking movement that used the whole stage rather than the lit center. The lighting designer noted that the new fixtures, though brighter, required careful dimming to preserve the shadows the company relied on.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A change in lighting technology altered how the company staged its performances.
The new fixtures were dimmer than the old ones.
The theater removed all shadows from its stage.
Audiences objected to the new lighting.

questions.explanation: The passage connects the new fixtures to changes in blocking and to the designer's adjusted approach. The main idea is that the technology reshaped the staging.

distractor_rationales.B: The text calls the new fixtures brighter.
distractor_rationales.C: The designer worked to preserve shadows rather than eliminate them.
distractor_rationales.D: Audience reaction is not described.

questions.stimulus: Before industrial whaling, sailors recorded whale sightings in logbooks, often noting only that whales were numerous. Researchers combing these logs found that sightings clustered along particular currents. The clustering matches modern tracking of the whales' prey, suggesting the animals followed food rather than fixed migration routes.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Old sighting records suggest that whale movements followed food rather than a fixed route.
Sailors exaggerated the number of whales they saw.
Whales no longer migrate at all.
The logs prove that whaling caused the population to decline.

questions.explanation: The passage reports that sightings match the location of prey and draws a conclusion about food rather than fixed routes. That conclusion is the main idea.

distractor_rationales.B: The text treats the logs as usable evidence, not as exaggeration.
distractor_rationales.C: It describes movement patterns, not an end to migration.
distractor_rationales.D: Population decline is not discussed.

questions.stimulus: Seedlings grown in sterilized soil often wilt during a dry spell, while seedlings in soil containing mycorrhizal fungi keep growing. The fungi extend threadlike networks that reach water beyond the plant's roots, and they receive sugars in return. In a drought year, plots with intact fungal networks produced more saplings than plots where the soil had been turned.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fungal networks can help seedlings survive drought by extending their access to water.
Mycorrhizal fungi harm the seedlings they associate with.
Sterilizing soil improves seedling growth in dry conditions.
Saplings in disturbed plots grew more than those in intact plots.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that fungal threads reach water the roots cannot and reports better sapling survival where the networks were intact. That is the main claim.

distractor_rationales.B: The relationship is described as mutually beneficial.
distractor_rationales.C: Sterilized soil seedlings wilted, so sterilization did not improve growth.
distractor_rationales.D: Intact plots produced more saplings than disturbed plots.

questions.stimulus: Moths of one species rest on tree bark and range from pale to dark. In a forest where soot darkened the trunks, dark moths became more common over several decades. When air-quality rules later lightened the trunks, pale moths increased again. These shifts suggest that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: moths whose color contrasted with the bark were more likely to be caught by birds.
individual moths changed color as the bark darkened.
soot helped the moths find food more easily.
the species split into two separate populations.

questions.explanation: The population shifts track how well each color matches the bark, which points to visual predators selecting the conspicuous moths. The other options require mechanisms the passage does not support.

distractor_rationales.B: An individual moth cannot change its inherited color as bark darkens.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage is about camouflage, not food finding.
distractor_rationales.D: No splitting of the species is described.

questions.stimulus: In a greenhouse, seedlings planted in soil from an old meadow grew larger than seedlings in soil from a young lawn, even though both soils had the same nutrients and water. When the meadow soil was heated to kill microbes, its advantage disappeared. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: microorganisms in the meadow soil contributed to the seedlings' greater growth.
heating the soil added nutrients that the lawn soil lacked.
lawn soil cannot support seedlings under any conditions.
meadow plants grow faster than lawn plants in every soil.

questions.explanation: Because nutrients and water were equal, and killing microbes removed the advantage, the living organisms in the meadow soil are the remaining explanation.

distractor_rationales.B: Heating removed the advantage rather than creating one.
distractor_rationales.C: Lawn soil supported seedlings; they simply grew less.
distractor_rationales.D: The comparison is between soils, not between plant types.

questions.stimulus: Chemical residue inside cooking pots from a coastal settlement contained fats from both land animals and fish. The pots were found in households of similar size and age. This pattern suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the households used a mix of land and marine foods rather than specializing in one.
the settlement had no access to land animals.
fish were traded inland from the settlement.
the pots were used only for storage.

questions.explanation: Pots in comparable households held both kinds of fat, which points to mixed use rather than specialization. The other choices contradict the residue or add unsupported claims.

distractor_rationales.B: Land-animal fats were found, so the settlement did have access to them.
distractor_rationales.C: Trade is not mentioned in the passage.
distractor_rationales.D: The pots were used for cooking, as the residue shows.

questions.stimulus: Young birds of one species raised in isolation develop songs that lack the local dialect heard in the wild. When recordings of the dialect are played to them during a sensitive period, their songs come to match it. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: young birds learn dialect features from what they hear rather than from instinct alone.
dialects are inherited genetically from parents.
adult birds can no longer learn new songs.
isolation improves the accuracy of a bird's song.

questions.explanation: Isolated birds lacked the dialect, and hearing recordings restored it, which shows a learned component. That rules out a purely genetic explanation.

distractor_rationales.B: Inherited song would not depend on hearing recordings.
distractor_rationales.C: The study concerns young birds, not adult learning.
distractor_rationales.D: Isolated songs lacked the local dialect.

questions.stimulus: A northern community builds a road across a frozen lake each winter. Officials close the road when measured ice thickness falls below a set level, even if the surface looks solid. This policy assumes that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: visible surface conditions can hide ice too thin to support vehicles.
thick ice never melts during the winter.
drivers can judge ice thickness reliably by looking at it.
the road is used only during daylight hours.

questions.explanation: Closing the road despite a solid-looking surface implies that appearance is not a safe guide. That is the assumption behind measuring thickness.

distractor_rationales.B: No claim is made that ice never melts.
distractor_rationales.C: The policy exists precisely because looking is not enough.
distractor_rationales.D: The timing of use is not mentioned.

questions.stimulus: Gardeners in a neighborhood with older housing tested their soil and found elevated lead near building foundations. They moved vegetable beds away from the walls and added clean compost. Subsequent tests showed lower lead in the beds. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the beds' location and added soil, rather than the neighborhood as a whole, explained the earlier readings.
compost removes lead from the vegetables that grow in it.
lead occurs naturally throughout the neighborhood's soil.
the first tests were performed incorrectly.

questions.explanation: Lead was elevated only near foundations, and moving the beds plus adding clean soil lowered the readings, which points to local conditions rather than a neighborhood-wide problem.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage does not claim compost removes lead from plants.
distractor_rationales.C: The pattern near foundations suggests a local source, not a uniform natural level.
distractor_rationales.D: The change after relocating the beds supports the original tests rather than discrediting them.

questions.stimulus: Documents stored in a damp basement faded more than identical documents stored in a dry room. The ink in both sets was made from the same recipe. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: moisture accelerated the fading of the ink.
the basement documents were much older.
the ink recipe changed between the two sets.
light alone caused all of the fading.

questions.explanation: The documents and ink were the same, so the storage condition is the difference that explains the extra fading. Moisture is the only variable named.

distractor_rationales.B: Nothing indicates an age difference.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage says both sets used the same recipe.
distractor_rationales.D: Light conditions are not described as differing.

questions.stimulus: Lichen species differ in how much air pollution they tolerate. Surveys along a road found only tolerant species near the highway and a mix of tolerant and sensitive species farther away. This pattern suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: pollution levels decline with distance from the highway.
sensitive species prefer the soil beside roads.
tolerant species require polluted air to survive.
lichens move quickly from one site to another.

questions.explanation: Sensitive lichens appear only where pollution is lower, which implies a gradient away from the road. That is the inference the survey supports.

distractor_rationales.B: Sensitive species were absent near the road, the opposite of preferring it.
distractor_rationales.C: Tolerance does not mean a requirement for pollution.
distractor_rationales.D: Dispersal speed is not discussed.

questions.stimulus: A shoreline behind an oyster reef eroded less than a nearby shoreline without one. Waves reaching the first shore were measured as smaller. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the reef reduced wave energy before the waves reached the shore.
oysters cement loose sand into solid rock.
the second shoreline had softer soil.
erosion depends only on the height of the tide.

questions.explanation: Smaller waves arrived where the reef stood, and that shore eroded less, which points to the reef absorbing wave energy.

distractor_rationales.B: No cementing process is described.
distractor_rationales.C: Soil differences are not mentioned.
distractor_rationales.D: The comparison isolates the presence of the reef.

questions.stimulus: Bats of one species forage along unlit paths more than along paths lit all night. When lamps were fitted with shields that directed light downward, bat activity along those paths increased. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: light spilling sideways, not light itself, discouraged the bats.
bats avoid every kind of artificial light equally.
shields attracted more insects to the paths.
the bats changed their diet after the shields were added.

questions.explanation: The lamps still shone, but shielding the sideways spill restored activity, so the direction of the light mattered. That isolates spill rather than light in general.

distractor_rationales.B: The shielded paths were still lit and the bats returned.
distractor_rationales.C: Insect numbers are not measured in the passage.
distractor_rationales.D: Diet is not discussed.

questions.stimulus: Pressed specimens of one wildflower, collected over a century at the same site and stored identically, show earlier flowering dates in recent decades. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the plants have been flowering earlier than they did a century ago.
the collectors visited the site only in spring.
pressing the flowers altered the dates on the labels.
the species has stopped flowering at this site.

questions.explanation: With the site and storage held constant, the shift in recorded dates points to a real change in flowering time. That is the inference the evidence supports.

distractor_rationales.B: A spring-only collector could not produce the range of dates described.
distractor_rationales.C: Pressing does not change the collection date on a label.
distractor_rationales.D: The specimens document flowering, which continues.

questions.stimulus: Seeds of a shrub germinate readily after being heated to temperatures reached in a brush fire but rarely without heat. In unburned plots seedlings are scarce; in recently burned plots they are abundant. This suggests that
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: fire cues trigger germination in this species.
fire supplies all the nutrients the shrub needs.
heat kills most of the shrub's seeds.
the shrub requires deep shade to reproduce.

questions.explanation: Seeds sprout after heat and seedlings follow fire, which indicates that fire acts as a germination cue. The other choices contradict the observation.

distractor_rationales.B: Nutrients are not measured in the passage.
distractor_rationales.C: Heated seeds germinated readily rather than dying.
distractor_rationales.D: Seedlings were abundant in burned, open plots.

questions.stimulus: A repair cafe invites volunteers to fix broken appliances for free. A city report opens by describing the tons of small electronics discarded each year. It then describes a weekend cafe where volunteers repaired 60 of the 75 items brought in. The report concludes that repair events divert only a fraction of the waste stream but build skills that outlast the events.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It frames a large problem, presents a small-scale response to it, then qualifies that response's impact.
It compares two cities that run repair cafes.
It argues that volunteers are responsible for electronic waste.
It describes a repair process step by step in chronological order.

questions.explanation: The report moves from the scale of the waste problem to one event and then limits the claim while noting another benefit. That is the structure described.

distractor_rationales.B: Only one city's report is described.
distractor_rationales.C: The report credits volunteers with repairs, not with creating the waste.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage describes the report's parts, not a repair procedure.

questions.stimulus: For years researchers assumed that sleep simply rested the brain. A study then showed that participants who slept after learning a list recalled more words than those who stayed awake. A second study found that the benefit depended on deep sleep rather than total hours. Together the studies shifted the question from whether sleep matters to which stage does the work.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It traces a shift from a general assumption to a more specific research question.
It describes a single experiment in exhaustive detail.
It compares two theories and concludes that neither can be tested.
It offers practical advice for improving sleep.

questions.explanation: The passage starts with an old assumption, reports two studies, and ends by naming a narrower question. That progression is the structure.

distractor_rationales.B: Two studies are summarized briefly, not one in detail.
distractor_rationales.C: The research is described as testable and productive.
distractor_rationales.D: No advice about sleep habits is given.

questions.stimulus: Early maps of a river delta show channels that no longer exist. A later map, drawn after a flood, shows a single channel. The text notes that the earlier channels were not errors: the delta itself had changed between surveys.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It explains why two maps that appear to disagree can both be accurate.
It argues that one of the maps is a deliberate fraud.
It describes the printing techniques used to make maps.
It compares the colors used by two mapmakers.

questions.explanation: The text reconciles the two maps by explaining that the landscape changed, so the apparent disagreement is not an error. That reconciliation is its structure and purpose.

distractor_rationales.B: The text explicitly says the earlier channels were not errors.
distractor_rationales.C: Printing methods are not mentioned.
distractor_rationales.D: Color is not discussed.

questions.stimulus: Many people assume that fermentation is a form of spoilage. The passage explains that in fermentation specific microbes outcompete the organisms that cause rot, and that the resulting acidity preserves food. It then notes that the same process can fail when temperatures favor the wrong microbes.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It corrects a common misconception and then notes a condition under which the process fails.
It gives a history of fermentation techniques.
It compares two recipes for the same food.
It argues that fermentation is unsafe in all cases.

questions.explanation: The passage first separates fermentation from rot and then adds a failure condition. That correction-then-qualification sequence is the structure.

distractor_rationales.B: No historical development is traced.
distractor_rationales.C: Recipes are not compared.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage presents fermentation as a preserving process, not an unsafe one.

questions.stimulus: One museum labels objects with dates and materials only. Another writes labels that begin with a question and end with an unresolved detail. The passage describes visitors spending longer at the second museum's cases and argues that the difference lies less in the objects than in the invitation to look closely.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It contrasts two labeling approaches and attributes a difference in visitor behavior to that contrast.
It argues that museums should remove labels entirely.
It describes a single exhibit in detail.
It compares the ticket prices of two museums.

questions.explanation: The passage sets one labeling style against another and explains the difference in attention by that contrast. That comparison-and-attribution is the structure.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage discusses two kinds of labels, not their removal.
distractor_rationales.C: No single exhibit is described in detail.
distractor_rationales.D: Ticket prices are not mentioned.

questions.stimulus: The passage lists the benefits of street trees: shade, cooler air, and slower storm runoff. It then observes that trees planted in narrow pits often die within a decade, and that cities which count only initial plantings overstate their progress.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It presents benefits and then qualifies a common way of measuring success.
It argues that street trees are not worth planting.
It compares two species of street tree.
It gives step-by-step planting instructions.

questions.explanation: After listing advantages, the passage points out that counting plantings alone can exaggerate progress. That is a qualification of a success measure.
